Typecheck reliability is undermined by resource constraints, creating a verification gap where syntactic validity masquerades as semantic integrity. This leads to a failure mode where type errors are silently ignored, especially when the compiler is killed. The derived kernel of this primitive is the notion that static guarantees are insufficient without runtime confirmation. The system's architecture assumes correctness through type safety, yet the type layer is not verified, introducing epistemic entropy. In GSI, this manifests as unreliable trust calibration; in GSE, it results in unvalidated state transitions. The retrocausal genealogy traces back to early software engineering principles where static analysis was considered a proxy for correctness, but modern systems demand both. The theory of mind involves adversarial agents who exploit this gap—either through malicious input or accidental misconfiguration. Anti-collinearity vetoes this by ensuring that static and dynamic layers do not coalesce into a single, unverifiable signal.
